newsitem.title: CROATIA: UN confirms election date in Croatian Serb enclave.
newsitem.headline: UN confirms election date in Croatian Serb enclave.

text.p: Jacques Klein, U.N. transitional administrator in a Serb enclave due to revert to Croatian state rule soon, confirmed on Tuesday that elections would be held there on April 13.

Klein had wanted to conduct the vote on the same day as nationwide elections for municipal councils and the upper House of Counties in the Croatian parliament, so his announcement of the timing was no surprise.

Election Day in the enclave was proclaimed after a meeting in Vukovar between Klein and members of the joint electoral implementation committee including Croatian Administration Minister Davor Mlakar, local Serb envoy Milos Vojnovic and the local U.N. election officer, Onofre dos Santos.
Klein told a news conference after the meeting that lists of candidates must be submitted by March 25.

A new party to represent local Serbs in the elections was formed only last week after former patron Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic told them they had no choice but to accept reintegration without "state-within-a-state" autonomy.

Minority Serbs seized Eastern Slavonia and two other enclaves in western Croatia in a 1991 revolt against independence from Serbian-led federal Yugoslavia, drove out Croat residents and declared a mini-state.

The Croatian army retook the two western enclaves in 1995 attacks over U.N. truce lines but called off a blitz on Eastern Slavonia after a temporary U.N. regime was conceived by U.S. diplomats, safeguarding Bosnia's new peace at the same time.

Vojislav Stanimirovic, a moderate, was elected president of the new Serb party on Monday, defeating nationalist hardliners opposed to reintegration in a decision that was greeted with relief by the U.N. Transitional Authority in Eastern Slavonia (UNTAES).

The Croatian government has promised the East Slavonian Serbs wide-ranging minority rights short of self-rule which would prevent Croats driven out in a 1991 war from returning to resettle their homes.
U.N. sources said Zagreb had also agreed to redraw a few of several dozen municipal districts at the Serbs' request to help them gain local majorities in the elections.
UNTAES spokesman Doug Coffman told Reuters that only 37 percent of eligible Serb voters in the fertile, oil-rich region had so far registered under Croatian law to vote.
"But we expect the rate to pick up now that the new Serb party has been formed. We expect more people will wake up now and pay attention to the approaching elections," he said.

About 120,000 Serbs are thought to inhabit Eastern Slavonia but ten of thousands are refugees from elsewhere in former Yugoslavia who will have to cede place after reintegration to Croats who formed a regional majority before the 1991 war.
International authorities want Croatia to resettle Serb refugees in western areas from which they were driven by Croatian army offensives against rebel territory in 1995.
More than 80,000 Serbs in Eastern Slavonia have obtained Croatian citizenship papers so far in a sign of growing willingness to stay and accept co-existence with Croats.
Croatian administrative, security and economic institutions will be phased in after the elections and almost all of 80,000 former Croat residents are expected to move back in again.
